final_proof:
Let $\struct{R, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity $1_R$. We first show that $g: \Z \to R$ given by $g(n) = n 1_R$ is a ring homomorphism.
For any $m, n \in \Z$:
$g(m + n) = (m + n)1_R = m 1_R + n 1_R = g(m) + g(n)$
$g(mn) = (mn)1_R = m(n 1_R) = m(1_R(n 1_R)) = (m 1_R) \circ (n 1_R) = g(m) \circ g(n)$
Thus, $g$ is a ring homomorphism. The image of $g$, denoted $g(\Z)$, consists of all integer multiples of $1_R$. Any subring of $R$ containing $1_R$ must contain $1_R + 1_R + \dots + 1_R = n 1_R$ for $n > 0$, their additive inverses for $n < 0$, and $0 1_R = 0_R$. Hence, $g(\Z)$ is contained in every subring of $R$ containing $1_R$. Since $g(\Z)$ is itself a subring, it is exactly the subring $S$ generated by $1_R$. Because the codomain of $g$ can be restricted to $S$ and $g$ maps onto $S$, $g$ is an epimorphism from $\Z$ onto $S$.

Now, suppose $R$ has no proper zero divisors. We will show that $g$ is the only nonzero homomorphism from $\Z$ into $R$. Let $h: \Z \to R$ be any nonzero homomorphism. Because $h$ is nonzero, there exists some $x \in \Z$ such that $h(x) \neq 0_R$.
Since $h$ is a homomorphism, $h(x) = h(x \cdot 1) = h(x) \circ h(1)$.
Thus, $h(x) \circ h(1) - h(x) = 0_R$, which factors as $h(x) \circ (h(1) - 1_R) = 0_R$.
Since $R$ has no proper zero divisors and $h(x) \neq 0_R$, we must have $h(1) - 1_R = 0_R$, so $h(1) = 1_R$.
Then, for any $n \in \Z$, $h(n) = h(n \cdot 1) = n h(1) = n 1_R = g(n)$. Thus $h = g$. (This also implies $g$ is nonzero, meaning $1_R \neq 0_R$, so $R$ is not the trivial ring).

Finally, we determine the kernel of $g$, $\ker(g)$. Since $\ker(g)$ is an ideal of $\Z$, and $\Z$ is a principal ideal domain, $\ker(g) = \ideal m$ for some integer $m \ge 0$. By the First Isomorphism Theorem for Rings, $S \cong \Z / \ker(g) = \Z / \ideal m$.
Because $R$ has no proper zero divisors, its subring $S$ also has no proper zero divisors. 
The quotient ring $\Z / \ideal m$ has proper zero divisors if $m$ is composite (since $m = ab$ with $1 < a, b < m$ gives nonzero classes $[a]$ and $[b]$ whose product is $[0]$). Also, $m$ cannot be $1$, because if $m=1$ then $S \cong \Z / \ideal 1$ is the trivial ring, which would mean $1_R = 0_R$, contradicting the fact that $R$ admits a nonzero homomorphism.
Thus, $m = 0$ or $m = p$ for some prime $p$.
Case (1): $m = 0$, so $\ker(g) = \ideal 0$. (This corresponds to $\ideal{0_R}$ in the problem statement, adopting the notation of the ring). In this case, $\Z / \ideal 0 \cong \Z$, so $g$ is an isomorphism from $\Z$ onto $S$.
Case (2): $m = p$ for some prime $p$, so $\ker(g) = \ideal p$. In this case, $S \cong \Z / \ideal p = \Z_p$. Since $p$ is prime, $\Z_p$ is a field, so $S$ is isomorphic to the field $\Z_p$.
This completes the proof.
